examples.title: Filtering Rows
examples.description: Keep only the rows that match a condition
examples.markdown:
## WHERE

`WHERE` works its condition out for every row, true or false, and keeps the rows where it is true.
cells:
-- Only the chocolate cones
SELECT * FROM cones WHERE Flavor = 'chocolate';

examples.title: Two Conditions
examples.description: Combine conditions with AND and OR
examples.markdown:
## AND, OR

`AND` needs both conditions to be true; `OR` needs either.

examples.title: Choosing Columns
examples.description: List the columns you want, or work new ones out
examples.markdown:
## SELECT

`SELECT` lists the result's columns. A column can be worked out from others; `AS` names it.
cells: SELECT Flavor, Price * 100 AS cents FROM cones;

examples.title: Distinct Rows
examples.markdown:
## DISTINCT

`DISTINCT` keeps one copy of each different row. Two pink strawberry cones become one.
cells: SELECT DISTINCT Flavor, Color FROM cones;

examples.title: Sorting
examples.description: Put rows in order of a column
examples.markdown:
## ORDER BY

`ORDER BY` sorts the rows; `DESC` puts the largest first.
cells: SELECT * FROM cones ORDER BY Price DESC;

examples.title: Top Three
examples.description: Sort, then keep the first rows
examples.markdown:
## LIMIT

`LIMIT` keeps the first rows of the result. With `ORDER BY` first, that is the top three.
cells:
-- The three priciest cones
SELECT * FROM cones
ORDER BY Price DESC
LIMIT 3;

examples.title: Group and Average
examples.description: One row per group, with its average
examples.markdown:
## GROUP BY

`GROUP BY` gathers the rows with the same flavor. Each aggregate in `SELECT` (here `AVG`) is worked out for each group.

examples.title: Counting Rows
examples.description: How many rows each group has
examples.markdown:
## COUNT(*)

`COUNT(*)` counts the rows in each group.

examples.title: Filtering Groups
examples.description: HAVING keeps the groups that match
examples.markdown:
## HAVING

`WHERE` filters rows before they are grouped; `HAVING` filters the groups after.
cells:
-- Flavors with more than one cone
SELECT Flavor, COUNT(*) AS cones
FROM cones
GROUP BY Flavor
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1;

examples.title: Summing Up a Table
examples.markdown:
## The whole table as one group

With no `GROUP BY`, aggregates combine every row into one.
cells:
SELECT COUNT(*) AS cones, AVG(Price) AS avg_price, MAX(Price) AS top_price
FROM cones;

examples.title: Joining Tables
examples.description: Match rows of two tables on a key
examples.markdown:
## JOIN

`JOIN ... ON` matches each cone with the freezer row of the same flavor. An inner join keeps only flavors found in both.
cells:
SELECT * FROM cones
JOIN stock ON cones.Flavor = stock.Flavor;

examples.title: Left Join
examples.description: Keep every row of the left table
examples.markdown:
## LEFT JOIN

A `LEFT JOIN` keeps every cone; flavors with nothing in the freezer get NULL for `Tubs`. `USING (Flavor)` joins on the column both tables share.
cells:
SELECT Flavor, Price, Tubs
FROM cones LEFT JOIN stock USING (Flavor);

examples.title: The Order SQL Runs In
examples.markdown:
## The order SQL runs in

A query is written SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY, LIMIT, but it runs FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY, LIMIT. The steps follow the order it runs in.
cells:
SELECT Flavor, AVG(Price) AS avg_price
FROM cones
WHERE Price > 4
GROUP BY Flavor
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1 OR AVG(Price) > 4.4
ORDER BY avg_price DESC
LIMIT 2;
